Chilean flamingos (Phoenicopterus chilensis) incubate their single egg for 28 days [ab = 28 days] at an average nest temperature of 37.2 °C [T = 37.2 °C], with the incubation period typically ranging from 26 to 31 days depending on ambient conditions and parental attentiveness. Upon hatching, the neonate emerges with a wet weight at birth of 85 grams [Wwb = 85 grams], a relatively substantial mass for an altricial chick that relies heavily on parental provisioning during its first weeks of life. The hatchling is brooded intensively by both parents, with the nest temperature maintained remarkably stable during the early critical phase by the parents' brood patches. This initial investment in a slowly maturing chick is characteristic of the genus, reflecting a life-history strategy that prioritizes offspring quality over quantity.

Under the relatively stable thermal conditions of their high-altitude breeding lakes, where effective body temperatures approximate 39.5 °C [T = 39.5 °C] during active foraging and brooding, developing chicks join the creche at around 67 days after hatching [tx = around 67 days after hatching], a milestone that marks fledging and the attainment of initial flight capability. This age at fledging is notably protracted compared to many other wading birds of similar adult body size, reflecting the energetic demands of growing the specialized filtering apparatus and the long, gangly legs required for wading. The chicks remain under communal adult supervision within these creches for several additional weeks, gradually learning to filter-feed independently while still receiving supplemental crop milk from their parents. The transition from nestling dependence to fledgling independence is thus a gradual process, with the 67-day threshold representing the point at which sustained flight becomes possible.

Under thermal conditions approximating 39.5 °C [T = 39.5 °C], sexual maturation occurs considerably later than fledging, with incubation data and field observations of known-age individuals indicating that puberty is reached at approximately 201 days after hatching [tp = approximately 201 days after hatching]. This timing corresponds to the point at which young flamingos first begin to participate in the synchronized courtship displays typical of the species, although successful breeding is not attempted until much later. The attainment of adult body mass is a prerequisite for gonadal development; females achieve an ultimate wet weight of 2530 grams [Wwi = 2530 grams], while males are considerably larger, reaching an ultimate wet weight for males of 3574 grams [Wwi = 3574 grams]. This degree of sexual size dimorphism is among the most pronounced in the family Phoenicopteridae and likely reflects divergent selective pressures on the sexes related to dominance in competitive displays.

The first successful breeding event among Chilean flamingos typically occurs at six years after hatching [tR = six years after hatching], a deferral that represents a significant investment in somatic development before any reproductive outp at a temperature of 39.5 °C [T = 39.5 °C]ut. Reproductive frequency is low, with females producing a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch] approximately once per year [F_R_i = approximately once per year], a rate that is among the lowest recorded for any colonial waterbird. This maximum reproduction rate of 1 clutch per year [F_R_i = 1 clutch per year] is constrained by the extreme energetic cost of producing a large, nutrient-rich egg and the protracted period of biparental care that follows hatching. Such a slow life-history pace is well suited to the unpredictable and often harsh environmental conditions of the high-altitude Andean lakes where the species breeds, where years of poor resource availability may preclude breeding entirely.

Maximum lifespan is considerable for a bird of this body size, with the oldest documented individuals surviving approximately 47 years [am = approximately 47 years] in captivity under stable thermal conditions near 39.5 °C [T = 39.5 °C], and field records suggesting a similar potential longevity in wild populations. This extended lifespan, coupled with the very low annual reproductive output, positions the Chilean flamingo as an extreme example of a slow life-history strategy within the Charadriiformes. The species' delayed maturity, extended parental care, and substantial investment in each individual offspring reflect an evolutionary adaptation to environments where adult survival is prioritized over high fecundity. Comparative studies with the smaller and earlier-maturing Lesser flamingo (Phoeniconaias minor) highlight how variation in body size and ecological niche within the flamingo lineage drives marked differences in these key life-history parameters.
